title: Greek tragedy and ancient theater
subtitle: 5th century BC AD
subject: art
description: In Athens, Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides invented tragedy. Choir, hubris, catharsis: a theater for thinking about the city.

hero.hook: Masks under the sun to heal the city through shock.

blocks.text: In the 5th century BC, in Athens, the **tragedy** was born. It is not a private entertainment: it is a civic rite, performed in front of thousands of citizens.
Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides invented an art that mixed gods, politics and passions.
The  sings, dances, comments. The actors, masked, embody heroes and gods. A rich citizen finances the show: it's the . [[The chorus in Greek tragedy]] [[choreogy]]
The Dionysia, festivals of Dionysus, organize competitions. The tragedy arises in this religious and civic framework. Winning means honoring the city as much as the god.

blocks.text: The tragic hero often gives in to , the excess that defies order. The fall that follows is not gratuitous: it questions justice, destiny, responsibility. [[hubris]]
Aeschylus adds actors; Sophocles refines psychology; Euripides disturbs certainties. Three styles for the same machine: making people think while moving.
sometimes had a god lowered by a crane to resolve the plot...already criticized for its convenience. [[deus ex machina]]
According to Aristotle, tragedy causes : a purification through pity and terror. We leave shaken, but peaceful. Theater heals the city by staging its fears. [[catharsis]]
The public often knows the myth. The interest isn't the twist, it's the manner. How will Oedipus fall? How will Antigone say no?

blocks.text: Shakespeare, opera, cinema: Greek tragedy remains the grammar of destiny on stage. Our modern antiheroes still owe their downfalls to him.
To fully understand Greek tragedy and ancient theater, you must keep one thing in mind: each technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never just decorative.
Context matters as much as style. Dates, places, sponsors, public: all this explains why a form appears at a specific moment, and not before.
Finally, legacy is measured over the long term. What we see today in museums, films or popular music still bears the traces of these inventions.
From Wagnerian opera to disaster cinema, the tragic structure survives. We have changed gods; not always falls.
In Athens, tragedy invented a civic theater where hubris, chorus and catharsis teach the city to look at itself.
